chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Floor shows and dancers at the Savoy and on the road
summary: Welburn asks about dancers; McRae describes late-night show numbers at the Savoy and road ballroom shows with Chick, Taft and Ella.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Well, how -- Just to -- has on a side here, you instituted this crowd pleasing device --
Yeah. Well, we did that --

-- with Lionel Hampton's band. But what I was interested in knowing is, to what degree did the musicians of the Chick Webb era -- when you were with Chick's band and later, of course, Lunceford's band, Cab's band -- how much attention did the musicians pay to the dancers? Or, did you have -- were there dancers at all the programs -- all the shows that you presented? Did some people stand around?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Oh, yeah.
Did a lot of people stand around and listen to the music --
Well they did that at the Savoy before we went on the road. In the Savoy, we used to put on -- not as much as (inaudible). Now in New York, the Savoy was different.

Every once in a while, we used to put on a show in New York. Maybe just about eleven o'clock at night when everybody was there. We would put on -- something that we play on the stage, something that we would try -- Say, we gonna go in a theater. We had worked out these openings. Opening number for a band, you know.

And we wanted to see how it would go over. But we would -- about 11:30 at night when the place was packed, you know, and the floor was packed, we would go into one of these big opening numbers -- something we gonna open at the Apollo Theater or the Paramount, something like that -- when we rehearsed
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

them, we used to play everything late at night.
We say, "This is gonna be the second band number." Sometimes these numbers would be so fast -- be up tempo, (inaudible) the floor would be packed, that you couldn't dance to them.
People would stand around and watch us go through this whole big arrangement. And when we got through, they say, "Oh, great," you know. Wonderful, you know.
See it go over big, then we go into a regular dance number.
Now on the road, we'd do something different. We would actually give the people a whole show in a ballroom.
Just before Ella come on, we would go into Chick's opening number, Taft would do "Sunny Side of the Street."
Maybe if Louie was there, he would do something. The band would come back and do -- Chick would come back and do his big number, understand?
And people would -- the whole ballroom just stand around looking, you know. Looking at the

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

show we was putting on. Chick would go through all his drums and all this stuff like that. Right after that, he would bring Ella on with a big number, "Tisket A-Tasket," or something. (Inaudible), Then she go into something else and do a real thing, you know --
All this time, the audience is --
Just standing there watching --
-- watching and appreciating he show.
This is the whole forty-five show before we take intermission. Then we go into a theme song and announce we're taking intermission (inaudible). Just like a floor show. We used to do that --
A lot of bands used to do that. Hamp used to do that, too. Hamp used to go through that "Flying Home" thing, you know, with Arnett Cobbs, with the small band down in front.

Then we used to do Boogie -- "Beulah's Boogie." You know, Milt Buckner on the piano doing that thing, you know, (inaudible).
I wrote another thing, "Beulah's Boogie No. 2 for him (inaudible). Same thing, just another extension part, but just a little bit different, you know.
